query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten fiber–reinforced tungsten (Wf/W) composites for fusion plasma-facing components, a single interfacial parameter—the fiber/matrix interfacial shear strength relative to the matrix flow stress at temperature—governs both high-temperature plastic strain and fracture toughness. When this ratio is in an intermediate window, controlled interfacial sliding activates extrinsic toughening (crack deflection, bridging, fiber pullout) and distributed inelasticity, which simultaneously increases plastic strain to failure and toughness. If the interface is too strong, cracks cut straight through (brittle, low plasticity and toughness); if too weak, load transfer is lost (reduced strength and diminished toughening).
generation.material_initial_state: Recrystallized tungsten matrix infiltrated around continuous W fibers (same fiber volume fraction and architecture across samples), high purity, identical grain size distribution in the matrix, no prior irradiation, interfaces either metallurgically bonded (as-processed) or coated as described in the intervention.
generation.intervention: Systematically tune the fiber/matrix interfacial shear strength by applying controlled thin interphases to the W fibers before matrix formation: e.g., (i) none (strongly bonded), (ii) ~50–200 nm boron carbide or pyrolytic carbon (intermediate debond/sliding), (iii) ~50–200 nm oxide/glass-like layer that greatly reduces shear strength (very weak). Keep fiber volume fraction, fiber architecture, matrix composition and grain size constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing in inert atmosphere or high vacuum to avoid oxidation, temperature 900–1200 C, nominal strain rate 1e-4–1e-3 s^-1. Fracture tests at the same temperatures. Unirradiated or very low-dose specimens (no significant helium bubble formation).
generation.structural_mediator: Fiber/matrix interfacial shear strength and the ratio of this shear strength to the matrix yield/flow strength at temperature; associated interfacial sliding distance/work capacity.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate interfacial shear strength, microcracks at the crack tip debond the interface and promote controlled fiber/matrix sliding and crack deflection, generating bridging tractions and fiber pullout that raise the crack growth resistance (extrinsic toughening). The same interfacial sliding also distributes inelastic deformation away from the crack tip and through the gauge section, enabling larger macroscopic plastic strain even when the high-temperature matrix alone would localize or cavitate. Interfaces that are too strong suppress debonding, forcing cracks through the brittle matrix/fiber with limited plasticity, while interfaces that are too weak unload fibers prematurely and truncate pullout/bridging, reducing both toughness and useful plastic strain.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a strongly bonded interface, composites with an intermediate-strength debonding/sliding interface will show: (a) higher uniform and total plastic strain at 900–1200 C; (b) higher high-temperature fracture resistance (rising J–R curve or higher KJQ); (c) a transition in fracture surface morphology from transgranular cleavage/shear in the matrix to pronounced fiber pullout and bridging; and (d) more stable, distributed inelastic deformation (less strain localization). Composites with very weak interfaces will show reduced ultimate strength and a decline in toughness compared to the intermediate case due to early fiber debonding and limited bridging.
generation.baseline: Monolithic recrystallized tungsten of the same purity and grain size tested under the same conditions, and a Wf/W composite with fully metallurgically bonded interfaces (no interphase).
generation.boundary: Expected to hold for continuous-fiber Wf/W composites with similar fiber aspect ratio and volume fraction, tested in non-oxidizing environments at temperatures where the matrix retains sufficient strength to transfer load to fibers and interfacial sliding remains activated (approximately 800–1300 C for typical W microstructures) and at quasi-static strain rates. May break down if: (i) interfaces chemically evolve (oxidize) or sinter during exposure, (ii) very high temperatures or very low strain rates lead to dominant matrix creep that overwhelms interface-controlled mechanisms, (iii) significant neutron/ion-induced helium or hydrogen bubbles nucleate at interfaces or grain boundaries altering sliding/cohesion, or (iv) fiber architectures are discontinuous/short or volumes are too low to provide bridging.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative bounds for the optimal interfacial shear strength window and the magnitude of improvements in plastic strain and toughness depend on specific fiber architectures, matrix grain size, and test conditions; without controlled comparative data here, only directional trends and the presence of an optimum at intermediate interfacial strength are asserted.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate at least three Wf/W composite cohorts differing only in interfacial shear strength: strong (no interphase), intermediate (thin B4C or pyrolytic carbon interphase), and very weak (WOx/glassy interphase), with identical fiber volume fraction, architecture, and matrix grain size. Measure interfacial shear strength independently via microbond or fiber push-in/out tests at temperature. Perform high-temperature tensile tests to failure and high-temperature fracture tests (e.g., compact tension J–R curves) at 1000 C in vacuum/inert gas. Conduct post-mortem fractography to quantify fiber pullout lengths and bridging. Include monolithic W as an external baseline.
measurements: Interfacial shear strength at test temperature (microbond or push-out)
True stress–strain curves at 1000 C (uniform and total elongation, flow stress)
High-temperature J–R curves or KJQ values
Acoustic emission signatures of debonding/bridging during loading
Fractography: fraction of surface area with fiber pullout, average pullout length, evidence of crack deflection/bridging
Creep or load relaxation during hold segments (to assess matrix-dominated behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either: (1) varying the measured interfacial shear strength does not produce the predicted non-monotonic trend with a maximum in both plastic strain and fracture toughness at intermediate interfacial strength (i.e., the intermediate-strength cohort does not outperform the strongly bonded cohort in both metrics and is not superior to the very weak cohort in toughness), or (2) the fracture surfaces and in-situ signals do not show a corresponding switch to fiber pullout/bridging in the intermediate-strength cohort.
